extracted.intended_audience: novelists and fiction writers (writers planning subplots)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical rules for creating, integrating, and resolving subplots in a novel so they add depth without undermining the main plot. Focuses on types of subplots, how they should connect to the main story, how many to include, and when to cut or spin off a subplot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplots follow a narrative arc
rubrics_metrics.description: All subplots should follow a narrative arc of conflict, crisis, and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states subplots should have the same basic structure as the main plot (conflict → crisis → resolution) and are usually wrapped up before the main plot’s climax. Treat subplots as smaller, self-contained arcs even if they run throughout the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplots must be connected to the main plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Your subplots must all be connected; a subplot that doesn’t have any bearing on or effect to the final denouement should be cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of weaving separate strands into a single cloth — each subplot should affect the ending or illuminate the main plot. If it does not influence the final outcome, consider removing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mirror subplot (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: A secondary conflict that mirrors the main conflict but usually doesn’t exactly match it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a best friend who also falls in love but with a different outcome; the mirror subplot helps the protagonist learn something about her own situation. Use to reflect themes or lessons without duplicating the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast subplot (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot that shows opposite progress or growth from the main plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the main character a weakness to overcome and show a secondary character who refuses to change. The contrast highlights the protagonist’s transformation by showing what happens when someone doesn’t grow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complications subplot (type)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot that complicates things for the main character and affects their trajectory toward the climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These subplots introduce obstacles (a 'monkey wrench') from outside the main plot and are useful for maintaining tension and keeping readers turning pages. They should still tie into the main plot’s outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subplots to add depth and momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots give your story depth and help keep it moving by introducing romances, family life, work concerns, friendships, internal conflicts, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subplots that reveal character, raise stakes, or introduce thematic complexity rather than filler. They should enrich reader understanding and propel narrative forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of subplots to avoid confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s no hard and fast rule, but too many subplots can create confusion for your reader and headaches for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb suggested: include a main conflict, an inner conflict, and a handful of subplots. If you find readers getting lost, trim or simplify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep subplots simpler than the main plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots should be simpler and have fewer steps to take for resolution than the main plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can introduce and resolve a subplot in a few chapters or thread it through to the end. Avoid building subplot arcs as complex as the main plot unless you intend to split them into separate works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve subplots by the end
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots shouldn’t be arbitrarily thrown in without careful thought and development; if a subplot shows up at the beginning of your story, make sure it’s resolved by the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unresolved early subplots frustrate readers. If a subplot cannot be tied up satisfactorily, consider removing it or saving it as the basis for another story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t let subplots hijack the main plot
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subplot is taking over, consider whether it should actually have a life of its own (the premise for your next story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the primacy of the main conflict. If a subplot grows too large or compelling, either scale it back or develop it separately to preserve story focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subplots to develop empathy and reveal interior life
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot can create empathy for your main character by showing vulnerability or a deep-seated desire they may not be aware of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ subplots (e.g., love interests, internal conflicts, coming-of-age elements) to deepen characterization and motivate protagonist choices, thereby reinforcing emotional stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thread subplots with recurring elements and clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Weave subplots into the narrative with recurring motifs, clues, or scenes so they resurface and pay off at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The To Kill a Mockingbird example: recurring mystery elements (trinkets in the knothole, blanket at the fire) fuel curiosity and then tie in at the conclusion. Plant seeds and revisit them so the subplot feels cohesive and earned.
